'''treacle-wormseed''' (trē′kl-wėrm″sēd), ''n.'' Same as ''treacle-mustard.''

'''treacliness''' (trē′kli-nes), ''n.'' Resemblance to treacle; viscosity. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The property of viscosity or ''treaclyness'' possessed more or less by all fluids is the general influence conducive to steadiness.
{{right|''Nature'', XXX. 89.}}}}

'''treacly''' (trē′kli), ''a.'' [< ''treacle'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Composed of or like treacle· abounding in treacle; sweet and viscous.

'''tread''' (tred), ''v.''; pret. ''trod'', pp. ''trod'', ''trodden'', ppr. ''treading.'' [< ME. ''treden'' (pret. ''trad'', pp. ''troden'', ''treden''), < AS. ''tredan'' (pret. ''træd'', pp. ''treden'') = OS. ''tredan'' = OFries. ''treda'' = D. ''treden'' = MLG. LG. ''treden'' = OHG. ''tretan'', MHG. G. ''treten'' = Icel. ''trodha'' = Sw. ''tråda'' = Dan. ''træde'' = Goth. ''trudan'', tread. The Icel. and Goth. show a different vowel. Hence ult. ''trade''<sup>1</sup>, ''trode'', ''trod.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To set the foot down, as on the ground.

{{smaller block|Ther nis, ywis, no serpent so cruel
Whan man ''tret'' on his tayl, ne half so fel,
As womman is, when she hath caught an ire.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Summoner's Tale, l. 294.}}
The smallest worm will turn being ''trodden'' on.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 2. 17.}}}}

'''2.''' To press or be put down on or as on the ground.

{{RunningHeader|treacher|6448|tread}}'''treacher†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''trecher'', ''trychor'', ''trecchour'', ''trechoure'', < OF. ''tricheor'', F. ''tricheur'' = Pr. ''trichaire'', ''trichador'' (cf. It. ''trecchiero''), < ML. ''tricator'', < ''tricare'', > OF. ''tricher'', ''trecher'', cheat, trick; see ''trick''1, ''v.'' For the relation of ''treacher'' to ''trick'', cf. that of ''lecher'', formerly also ''leacher'', to ''lick''. Cf. ''treachery''.] A traitor; a cheat; a deceiver. {{smaller block|Of alle the world is Emperour
Gyle my fadir, the ''trechour''. {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 7214.}} Play not two parts,
''Treacher'' and coward both. {{right|''Fletcher (and others)'', Bloody Brother, iii. 1.}}}} '''treacherer†''', ''n.'' [< ''treacher'' + ''-er'' (added superfluously, as in ''poulterer'', etc.).] Same as ''treacher''. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Whose deep ambitious reach was still implor'd
To raise more millions of ''treacherers'',
Of homicidial cruel slaughterers. {{right|''Ford'', Fame's Memorial.}}}} '''treacherous''' (trech′ėr-us), ''a.'' [< ''treacher'', ''treacher-y'' + ''-ous''.] 1. Using treachery; violating allegiance or faith pledged; traitorous to the state or sovereign; perfidious in private life; betraying a trust. {{smaller block|Thou common friend, that 's without faith or love,
For such is a friend now; ''treacherous'' man!
Thou hast beguiled my hopes. {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., v. 4. 63.}}}} 2. Marked by deceitfulness or perfidy; characteristic of a traitor. {{smaller block|You know I am not false, of a ''treacherous'' nature,
Apt to betray my friend; I have fought for you too. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Little French Lawyer, ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Was 't not a most ''treacherous'' part to arrest a man in the night, and when he is almost drunk? {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Westward Ho, iii. 2.}}}} 3. Having a good, fair, or sound appearance, but worthless or bad in character or quality; deceptive; not to be depended on or trusted. {{smaller block|The ''treacherous'' colours the fair art betray, And all the bright creation fades away! {{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 492.}}}} {{smaller block|To the foot ''Treach'rous'' and false; it [ice] smil'd, and it was cold. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, v. 176.}}}} {{smaller|='''Syn.''' 1. ''Faithless'', etc. (see ''perfidious''), recreant, treasonable.}} '''treacherously''' (trech′ėr-us-li), ''adv.'' In a treacherous manner; by treachery. {{smaller block|If you can't be fairly run down by the Hounds, you will be ''treacherously'' shot by the Huntsmen. {{right|''Congreve'', Love for Love, i. 2.}}}} '''treacherousness''' (trech′ėr-us-nes), ''n.'' The character of being treacherous; breach of faith or allegiance; faithlessness; perfidy. '''treachery''' (trech′ėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''treacheries'' (-iz). [< ME. ''trecherie'', ''treccherye'', ''tricherie'', < OF. ''tricherie'', ''trecherie'', F. ''tricherie'' (= Pr. ''tricharia'' = It. ''treccheria''), treachery, < ''tricher'', ''trichier'', ''trecher'', cheat: see ''trick''1, ''v.'' Cf. ''trickery''.] Violation of allegiance or of faith and confidence; treasonable or perfidious conduct; perfidy. {{smaller block|Now am I fawty, & falce, & ferde haf been euer; Of ''trecherye'' & vn-thawthe bothe bityde sorȝe. {{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2382.}}}} {{smaller block|I am the creatur that il kan fene Any falsed or ''trechere''. {{right|''Book of Precedence'' (E. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 87.}} Those that betray them do no ''treachery.'' {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 3. 24.}}}} =Syn. See ''perfidious.'' '''treachetour†''', ''n.'' [An erroneous form, a mixture of ''treachour'' and ''traitor'', perhaps confused with ''tregetour.''] A traitor. {{smaller block|The king was by a ''Treachetour'' Disguised slaine, ere any thereof thought. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. x. 51.}}}} '''treachour†''', ''n.'' Same as ''treacher.'' '''treacle''' (trē′kl), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''triacle;'' < ME. ''triacle,'' < OF. ''triacle'', treacle, F. ''thériaque'' = Pr. ''tiriaca, triacla'' = Sp. ''teriaca, triaca'' = Pg. ''theriaga, triaga'' = It. ''teriaca'', < L. ''theriaca'', < Gr. θηριακή (sc. ἀντίδοτος), an antidote against the (poisonous) bites of wild beasts: see ''theriac.''] 1. A medicinal compound of various ingredients, formerly believed to be capable of curing or preventing the effects of poison, particularly the effects of the bite of a serpent. See ''theriac.'' {{smaller block|And therefore I wel alowe your request in this behalf, that you would haue store of cumfort afore hand ready by you to resorte to, and to lay up in your hart as a ''triacle'' against the poyson of al desperate dread that might rise of occasion of sore tribulation. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Cumfort against Tribulation (1573), p. 5.}}}} {{smaller block|Having packed up my purchases of books, pictures, casts, ''treacle'', &c. (the making and extraordinary ceremony whereof I had been curious to observe, for it is extremely pompous and worth seeing), I departed from Venice. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, March 23, 1646.}}}} {{smaller block|''Treacle'', a Physical Composition, made of Vipers and other Ingredients. {{right|''E. Phillips'', 1706.}}}} 2. More generally, a remedy; a panacea; a sovereign antidote or restorative: often used figuratively. {{smaller block|Crist, which that is to every harm ''triacle''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law's Tale, l. 381.}}}} {{smaller block|Love is ''triacle'' of hevene. ''Piers Plowman'' (B), ii. 146.}} {{smaller block|The sovran ''treacle'' of sound doctrine. {{right|''Milton'', Church Government, ii., Conclusion.}}}} {{smaller block|There is, even for the most debauched drunkard that ever was, a sovereign medicine, a rich ''triacle'', of force enough to cure and recover his disease. {{right|''Rev. S. Ward'', Sermons, p. 157.}}}} 3. The spume of sugar in sugar-refineries: so called as resembling in appearance or supposed medicinal properties the ancient theriacal compounds. {{smaller|Treacle is obtained in refining sugar; molasses is the drainings of crude sugar. The name ''treacle'', however, is very often given to molasses.}} {{smaller block|Mrs. Squeers stood at one of the desks, presiding over an immense basin of brimstone and ''treacle'', of which delicious compound she administered a large instalment to each boy. {{right|''Dickens'', Nicholas Nickleby, viii.}}}} 4. A saccharine fluid consisting of the inspissated juices or decoctions of certain vegetables, as the sap of the birch or of the sugar-maple.—5. One of several plants sometimes regarded as antidotes to poison, or named from plants so regarded. See the phrases below.—{{smaller|'''Countryman's treacle,''' the common rue, ''Ruta graveolens''; also, the common valerian and garlic. [Prov. Eng.]—'''English treacle†''', the water-germander, ''Teucrium Scordium.''—'''Poor man's treacle.''' Same as ''churl's-treacle''; also, the garlic-mustard, ''Sisymbrium Alliaria'', and in England the onion, ''Allium Cepa.''—'''Venice treacle.''' See ''theriac.''}} '''treacle-mustard''' (trē′kl-mus″tä̤rd), ''n.'' See ''mustard.'' '''treacle-sleep''' (trē′kl-slēp), ''n.'' A sweet refreshing sleep. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|I fell first into a sluggish torpor, then into ''treacle-sleep'', and so lay sound. ''Carlyle'', in Froude (Life in London, viii.).}} '''treacle-wag''' (trē′kl-wag), ''n.'' Weak beer in which treacle is a principal ingredient. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] '''treacle-water''' (trē′kl-wâ″tėr), ''n.'' A compound cordial, distilled with a spirituous menstruum from any cordial and sudorific drugs and herbs, with a mixture of Venice treacle, or theriac. {{smaller block|To make ''treacle-water'', good in surfeits, &c.—Take the husks of green-walnuts, four handfuls; of the juice of rue, carduus, marigolds, and balm, of each a pint; green perasitis roots, one pound; angelica and masterwort, of each half a pound; the leaves of scordium four handfuls; old Venice-treacle and mithridate, of each eight ounces; six quarts of canary; of vinegar three quarts, and of lime-juice one quart: which being two days digested in a bath in a close vessel, distill them in sand. {{right|''The Closet of Rarities'' (1706). (''Nares.'')}}}} '''treacle-wormseed''' (trē′kl-wėrm″sēd), ''n.'' Same as ''treacle-mustard.'' '''treacliness''' (trē′kli-nes), ''n.'' Resemblance to treacle; viscosity. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The property of viscosity or ''treaclyness'' possessed more or less by all fluids is the general influence conducive to steadiness. {{right|''Nature'', XXX. 89.}}}} '''treacly''' (trē′kli), ''a.'' [< ''treacle'' + ''-y''1.] Composed of or like treacle· abounding in treacle; sweet and viscous. '''tread''' (tred), ''v.''; pret. ''trod'', pp. ''trod'', ''trodden'', ppr. ''treading.'' [< ME. ''treden'' (pret. ''trad'', pp. ''troden'', ''treden''), < AS. ''tredan'' (pret. ''træd'', pp. ''treden'') = OS. ''tredan'' = OFries. ''treda'' = D. ''treden'' = MLG. LG. ''treden'' = OHG. ''tretan'', MHG. G. ''treten'' = Icel. ''trodha'' = Sw. ''tråda'' = Dan. ''træde'' = Goth. ''trudan'', tread. The Icel. and Goth. show a different vowel. Hence ult. ''trade''1, ''trode'', ''trod.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To set the foot down, as on the ground. {{smaller block|Ther nis, ywis, no serpent so cruel Whan man ''tret'' on his tayl, ne half so fel, As womman is, when she hath caught an ire. {{right|''Chaucer'', Summoner's Tale, l. 294.}} The smallest worm will turn being ''trodden'' on. {{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 2. 17.}}}} '''2.''' To press or be put down on or as on the ground. {{smaller block|Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall ''tread'' shall be yours. {{right|Deut. xi. 24.}}}} 3. To walk; step; especially, to walk with a more or less stately, measured, or cautious step. {{smaller block|Whan they han goon nat fully half a myle, Ryght as they wolde han ''troden'' over a style. {{right|''Chaucer'', Pardoner's Tale, l. 250.}}}} {{smaller block|Has it a corn? or does it walk on conscience, It ''treads'' so gingerly? {{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Love's Cure, ii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|O welcome, Sir Oluf! now lat thy love gae, And ''tread'' wi' me in the dance sae gay. {{right|''Sir Oluf and the Elf-King's Daughter'' (Child's Ballads, I. 299).}}}} {{smaller block|On burnish'd hooves his war-horse ''trode''. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lady of Shalott.}}}} 4. To copulate, as birds: said especially of a cock-bird. {{smaller block|When turtles ''tread'', and rooks, and daws. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 915.}}}} '''To have the black ox tread on one's foot†.''' {{smaller|See ''ox.''}}—'''To tread awry.''' {{smaller|See ''awry.''}}—'''To tread in one's steps''' (or '''footsteps'''), to follow one closely; imitate one. {{smaller block|The boys take all after their father, and covet to ''tread in his steps.'' {{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim's Progress, ii.}}}} '''To tread on''' or '''upon.''' (''a'') To trample; set the foot on in contempt. {{smaller block|Thou shalt ''tread upon'' their high places. {{right|Deut. xxxiii. 29.}}}} (''b'') To follow closely. {{smaller block|Year ''treads on'' year. {{right|''Wordsworth.''}}}} '''To tread on one's toes,''' to vex, offend, interfere with, or hurt one. {{smaller block|Presently found he could not turn about Nor take a step i' the case and fail to ''tread'' ''On'' some ''one's toes.'' {{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 130.}}}} '''To tread on''' or '''upon the heels of,''' to follow close upon. {{smaller block|One woe doth ''tread upon'' another's ''heel.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 7. 164.}}}} '''To tread on the neck of.''' {{smaller|See ''neck.''}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To step or walk on. {{smaller block|My roof receives me not; 'tis air I ''tread''; And, at each step, I feel my advanced head Knock out a star in heaven! {{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, v. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|She herself had ''trod'' Sicilian fields. ''M. Arnold'', Thyrsis.}} 2. To beat or press with the feet: as, a well-''trodden'' path. {{smaller block|I have ''trodden'' the winepress alone. Isa. lxiii. 3.}} {{smaller block|They should have stabb'd me where I lay; . . . They should have ''trod'' me into clay. {{right|''Tennyson'', Oriana.}}}} 3. To crush under the foot; trample in contempt or hatred. {{smaller block|Through thy name will we ''tread'' them under that rise up against us. Ps. xliv. 5.}} {{smaller block|Cammomill ''trodden'' doth the farther spred, And the palme prest the higher lifts his head. {{right|''Times' Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 139.}}}} {{smaller block|We should not submit to be ''trodden'' quite flat by the first heavy-heeled aggressor that came along. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, iii.}}}} 4. To dance. {{smaller block|We have measured many miles To ''tread'' a measure with her on this grass. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 185.}}}} 5. To walk. {{smaller block|I am resolv'd To forsake Malta, ''tread'' a pilgrimage To fair Jerusalem, for my lady's soul. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, v. 2.}}}} 6. To copulate with or cover, as a bird. {{smaller block|What shall I say of the House-Cock, which ''treads'' any hen? ''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 47.}} {{smaller|'''To tread down''', to crush or destroy, as by trampling under foot.}} {{smaller block|Look on every one that is proud, and bring him low; and ''tread down'' the wicked in their place. Job xl. 12.}} '''To tread one's shoes straight,''' to walk straight; go carefully or discreetly; be circumspect. [Slang.] {{smaller block|And I've heard the old man say, sir, I was further told, how he had to ''tread his shoes straight'' about what books he showed publicly. {{right|''Mayhew,'' London Labour and London Poor, I. 318.}}}} '''To tread out.''' (''a'') To press out with the feet, as wine or grain. {{smaller block|Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he ''treadeth out'' the corn. {{right|Deut. xxv. 4.}}}} (''b'') To destroy, extinguish, or obliterate by or as by treading or trampling. {{smaller block|A little fire is quickly ''trodden out.'' {{right|''Shak.,'' 3 Hen. VI., iv. 8. 7.}}}} '''To tread the bounds.''' Same as ''to beat the bounds.'' See ''bound''1.—'''To tread the stage''' or '''the boards,''' to act as a stage-player; perform a part in a drama. {{smaller block|So once were rang'd the sons of ancient Rome, A noble show! while Roscius ''trod the stage.'' {{right|''Cowper,'' Task, iii. 597.}}}} '''To tread under foot,''' to trample on; despise; treat with contempt. {{smaller block|If ever men ''tread under foot'' the Son of God, it is when they think themselves to be above the need of him. {{right|''Stillingfleet,'' Sermons, I. vi.}}}} '''To tread water,''' in swimming, to move the feet and hands regularly up and down, while keeping the body in an erect position, in order to keep the head above the water. '''tread''' (tred), ''n.'' [< ''tread,'' ''v.'' Cf. ''trade''1.] 1. A step or stepping; footing; pressure with the foot. {{smaller block|She is coming, my own, my sweet; Were it ever so airy a ''tread,'' My heart would hear her and beat. {{right|''Tennyson,'' Maud, xxii. 11.}}}} {{smaller block|I cross my floor with a nervous ''tread.'' {{right|''Whittier,'' Demon of the Study.}}}} '''2'''†. Way; track; path. See ''trade''1, ''n.'', 2.—'''3'''. Copulation, as of birds.—'''4'''. The cicatricula of an egg: so called from the former erroneous belief that it appeared only in fecundated eggs laid by the hen after the tread of the cock. Compare
